name: deskyard
description: Use a Deskyard computer (a Linux desktop with a shared Chromium) from inside it or remotely through its server's API, after `deskyard login`. Run commands as `deskyard [-c COMPUTER] <name> <arguments...>`: the global -c COMPUTER or -c SERVER/COMPUTER (--computer) chooses the computer and goes before the command name; arguments are positional in the listed order, and a command's flags go after its name.

globalFlags.name: --computer
globalFlags.description: the computer to use: COMPUTER on the default server, or SERVER/COMPUTER (see `deskyard server list`); only before the command name

environment.name: DESKYARD_COMPUTER
environment.description: computer to use when -c isn't given (COMPUTER or SERVER/COMPUTER)

environment.name: DESKYARD_URL
environment.description: server URL, optionally with a computer (https://host/alice), to use instead of the default server; needs DESKYARD_CREDENTIAL

environment.name: DESKYARD_SETTLE
environment.description: seconds screenshot and zoom wait before capturing (default 0.3)

exitCodes.meaning: error (the message on stderr says what to do next)
usage error (bad command, flag or argument)
exec, shell and screen actions pass through the exit code of the command in the computer

commands.name: screenshot
commands.description: Takes a PNG screenshot of the whole screen, after a short settle delay (DESKYARD_SETTLE seconds, default 0.3) so the screen reflects your last action. Without FILE, or with -, the PNG goes to stdout. Take one before acting and after, to see what happened; coordinates in the image are screen coordinates.

arguments.name: file
arguments.description: where to write the PNG on this machine; - or omitted for stdout

output.description: PNG image bytes on stdout, or nothing when FILE is given (the file is written on this machine)

commands.where: inside a computer it acts locally; elsewhere on the chosen computer (-c COMPUTER)
commands.exitCodes: 0 ok, 1 error, 2 usage error; otherwise the exit code of the action on the desktop

arguments.name: file

commands.name: exec

commands.description: Runs one command as user (in /workspace unless --cwd) and streams its stdin, stdout and stderr; exits with the command's exit code. The command is run as given, not through a shell: for pipes, globs or && use `-- bash -lc '...'`.

output.description: the command's stdout and stderr as they arrive; with --json one object {"stdout":string,"stderr":string,"exit":int}, using "stdoutBase64"/"stderrBase64" (base64) instead when the output isn't UTF-8

fields.stdoutBase64: standard output, base64, when not UTF-8

examples: deskyard -c alice exec -e CI=1 -- make test
deskyard exec --json -- bash -lc 'cd app && npm test'

commands.name: terminal
commands.description: Joins a shared Bash login shell in /workspace, default main. Browser, CLI and desktop clients share the same session. Inside an existing native shared terminal, press Ctrl-B then s and choose the session instead of nesting this command. Detach with Ctrl-B then D; jobs survive disconnect but end when the computer restarts. Session names use 1–64 letters, digits, underscores or dashes and start with a letter or digit.

commands.description: Opens an interactive bash login shell in the computer in your terminal (raw mode, resizes follow your window). Exit with `exit` or Ctrl-D. For scripted use, prefer exec.

commands.name: cp
commands.summary: copy files to or from a computer
commands.description: Copies a file or directory between this machine and a computer; write the computer side as COMPUTER:/path (COMPUTER is a computer on the chosen server, -c SERVER/… or the default one; an empty COMPUTER, as in :/path, means the chosen computer). A file lands at DST, or inside DST when it is an existing directory. A directory's contents land in DST, which is created (like `cp -r SRC/. DST`). SRC - reads stdin; DST - writes to stdout (a tar stream for a directory). Files land as user; inside a computer, two local paths are copied locally.

output.description: nothing, unless DST is - (the file's bytes or a tar stream)

commands.exitCodes: 0 ok, 1 error, 2 usage error

commands.name: forward
commands.summary: map TCP ports between this machine and the computer
commands.description: Maps TCP ports both ways until Ctrl-C, over the remote access API (no port is opened anywhere else). Each argument is one mapping. PORT or LOCAL:COMPUTER: this machine's 127.0.0.1:LOCAL becomes localhost:COMPUTER in the computer (a dev server here, reachable by the computer's browser). -R PORT or -R COMPUTER:LOCAL (reverse; one -R before each such mapping): the computer's localhost:COMPUTER becomes 127.0.0.1:LOCAL here. Both ends listen on loopback only; the computer won't listen below 1024 (plain forward only; -R just dials, so -R 80:8080 works). A port in use on either side fails that mapping, which is retried, and the others carry on. When the connection drops (the computer stops or restarts, the network blips) it keeps its local listeners, closes open connections and reconnects with backoff (1 s up to 30 s). It exits only on Ctrl-C, or when the credential is refused. Run it in the background. Inside a computer it needs -c too.

arguments.name: port
arguments.description: a mapping: PORT or LOCAL:COMPUTER; after -R, PORT or COMPUTER:LOCAL

flags.name: --reverse
flags.description: the next mapping is reverse: a port in the computer becomes a port here

output.description: one line per mapping each time it goes live: "in LOCAL COMPUTER" or "out COMPUTER 127.0.0.1:LOCAL"; on stderr one line per state change (linked, lost and retrying, port in use)

fields.in: LOCAL COMPUTER: this machine's port, reachable in the computer at localhost:COMPUTER
fields.out: COMPUTER ADDR: the computer's port, reachable here at ADDR

commands.where: on the chosen computer (-c COMPUTER); inside a computer too, since it maps ports between two machines. Ports are LOCAL:COMPUTER, or COMPUTER:LOCAL after -R. The computer won't listen below 1024. "Linked to ..." and the out lines appear when the link is accepted, before the computer side is known to run
commands.exitCodes: 0 after Ctrl-C, 1 when the credential is refused (401) or no computer is chosen, 2 usage error

commands.name: browser connect
commands.summary: forward the computer's browser to a local CDP port
commands.description: Listens on 127.0.0.1:PORT and forwards the Chrome DevTools Protocol to the computer's shared Chromium (the one on its desktop, with your signed-in sessions), so Playwright, Puppeteer or DevTools tools connect as if the browser were local. Prints the URL, then keeps running until Ctrl-C. Run it in the background. Inside a computer it isn't needed: CDP is at http://127.0.0.1:9221.

flags.name: --port
flags.description: local port (0 = any free port)

output.description: first line: the local CDP URL (http://127.0.0.1:9222); connection log on stderr

commands.name: login
commands.summary: sign in to a server, approving in the browser
commands.description: Signs this CLI in to a Deskyard server: prints a code and an approval URL (on stderr) and opens it in your browser, where you check the code and approve while signed in to Deskyard. Then saves the server, your username and a client credential for this machine in servers.json ($XDG_CONFIG_HOME/deskyard, default ~/.config/deskyard; mode 0600). With a computer in the URL (https://host/alice) it becomes the server's default computer, once checked that you have full access to it; without one, your only computer does. The first server becomes the default. The request expires after 10 minutes.

arguments.name: url
arguments.description: the server's address, optionally with a computer: https://host or https://host/alice

flags.name: --name
flags.description: local name for the server, used with -c NAME/COMPUTER (default: its host name, unless another server already has it)

flags.name: --no-browser
flags.description: only print the approval URL, don't open a browser

output.description: a confirmation with the account and computer; the code and approval URL on stderr

When the account has exactly one computer it becomes the default. Observe-only links work in a browser only.

commands.name: computer create
commands.description: Creates a computer from an image and starts it, printing the progress (pulling the image, starting the desktop) on stderr until it is ready; Ctrl-C stops following, not the creation. Its files are in home/NAME/ in the server's data folder; a folder left by an earlier computer of that name is reused. Administrators have access to every computer; --grant gives it to other accounts.
